title: The bow
hookLine: back straight, hands on knees, glory to my Lord the Great

cards: A man walks into the mosque in Medina and prays, quickly. Then he comes over to the Prophet ﷺ and greets him with salaam.
The Prophet returns the greeting, and then says something the man didn't expect: go back and pray, because you haven't prayed. In a bow, the body can look finished before it has arrived.
A dip of the head and shoulders, and it's over. So what was that man missing?

teach.h: RUKU' — TO BEND, TO BOW DOWN.
teach.b: The bow is called ruku', from a root meaning to bend, to bow down. After the recitation, the person says Allahu akbar and bends forward from the hips, hands on the knees, back level, head in line with the back.
There, usually three times, they say: subhana rabbiya al-'azim.

teach.h: GLORY TO MY LORD, THE GREAT.
teach.b: Glory to my Lord, the Magnificent, the Great. A report in the Sunan says that when a verse came telling the Prophet to glorify the name of his Lord, the Tremendous, he said: put it in your bowing.
Now, the man in the mosque. The hadith is in Bukhari.

He went back and prayed, came again, and was told again: go back and pray, you haven't prayed. Three times. Finally he said: by the One who sent you with the truth, I don't know any better, so teach me.

teach.h: BOW UNTIL YOU ARE AT REST.
teach.b: Among the things he said: bow until you are at rest in your bowing. That's the missing piece. There's a word for it, tuma'nina: stillness, settling.
The body has to arrive in the bow before it leaves. A bow that's only a dip is a gesture.

teach.h: A BOW THAT SETTLES IS HONEST.
teach.b: A bow that settles says, with the whole spine, that the one bowing isn't in a hurry to stand back up. And in the tradition, a Muslim bows like this to God alone. Not to a king, not to a teacher, not to a parent.
That's the sense in which the bow is honest: it means what it shows, and it's aimed where the tradition says it belongs.

how: After reciting, Muslims say Allahu akbar and bow with hands on their knees and back level, usually saying subhana rabbiya al-'azim three times, and remaining still in the bow before rising.

o: a quick nod of the head to greet someone
the bow in prayer, hands on knees, still and settled
a deep bow of respect made to an elder or a teacher

games.q: what's inside the bow — tap the pairs.
p: glory to my Lord, the Great
told three times: go back and pray

s: a quick dip of the body is enough for the bow
the Prophet ﷺ taught: bow until you are at rest in your bowing.
in the tradition, this bow is for God alone
Muslims don't bow like this to kings, teachers or parents.
the words of the bow are made up by each person
the usual words are subhana rabbiya al-'azim, glory to my Lord the Great, often three times.

games.q: you've prayed quickly, and the Prophet ﷺ has sent you back three times, saying you haven't prayed. what do you do?
o: pray even faster, to get it done
say: I don't know any better, so teach me
games.why: the man asked to be taught, and the Prophet taught him, including: bow until you are at rest in your bowing (Bukhari).

practice: Stand, then bend forward from the hips, hands resting on your knees, back as level as it comfortably goes; if your back won't allow it, bow your head and shoulders instead. Stay there, and let your breath slow.
If you pray, you can say it three times, subhana rabbiya al-'azim, glory to my Lord the Great; if not, count three slow breaths, then stand, and sit.

wordCard.voice: Ruku'. The bow in prayer: back level, hands on knees, and still enough to be at rest. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: bowing, from a root meaning to bend or bow down.

carryVoice: Your line: bowing is honest. Stillness was the piece the hurried man was missing. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 757 (the man told to go back and pray; bow until at rest)
